slides.title: Asking nicely
slides.text: Ask nicely when you want a turn. Say "Can I play too?" instead of grabbing.

slides.title: Listening back
slides.text: Listen when your friend answers about the ball. Maybe they just need two more minutes to finish.

slides.title: Taking turns
slides.text: Take turns with a red truck you both want. Play five minutes, then let your friend play.

slides.title: Trading fair
slides.text: Trade toys so both of you feel happy about it. Swap your red crayon for your friend's blue crayon.

slides.title: Try a different idea
slides.text: If a friend says no, try a new idea. Ask, "Can we play this toy together instead?"

slides.title: Both people give a little
slides.text: A compromise means you both get some of what you want. Play tag first, then play hide and seek.

slides.title: Say please and thank you
slides.text: Say please when you ask, and thank you after. Even a "no" can still feel kind and friendly.

slides.title: Know what you want first
slides.text: Think about what you really want before you ask. That makes it easier to ask for the right thing.

slides.title: It's okay to hear no
slides.text: Sometimes people will tell you no. It is okay — stay calm and try again later.

slides.title: Sharing the tablet
slides.text: You and your sibling both want the tablet. Take turns, ten minutes each, so it feels fair.

slides.title: Chores can be split
slides.text: Two people can share one big job. You pick up toys, your sibling wipes the table.

slides.title: Walking away from a bad deal
slides.text: If a trade feels bad, you can say no. Walk away and find something better to do.

quiz.question: What is the first step to getting a yes when you want something?
choices: Asking nicely
Grabbing it
quiz.explanation: Asking nicely, instead of grabbing or shouting, is the first step.

quiz.question: You ask for the ball and your friend says "in two minutes." What should you do?
choices: Listen to what the other person says
Cover your ears
quiz.explanation: Listening back helps you understand their reason or idea.

quiz.question: You and a friend both want the same red truck. What can you do?
choices: Take turns
Fight over it
quiz.explanation: Taking turns means everyone gets to play with it.

quiz.question: You trade your red crayon for a friend's blue one. What should a trade feel like?
choices: Fair to both people
Only good for one person
quiz.explanation: A good trade feels fair to both people involved.

quiz.question: You want tag, your friend wants hide and seek, so you agree to play both. What is this called?
choices: A compromise — both people give a little
Only one person gets what they want
quiz.explanation: In a compromise, both people give a little and both get something.

quiz.question: Before you ask for something, what should you do first?
choices: Think about what you really want
Just grab it right away
quiz.explanation: Thinking first helps you ask for the right thing.

quiz.question: Your friend says no. What should you do?
choices: Stay calm and try again later
Yell and grab it
quiz.explanation: Staying calm keeps things friendly, even after a no.

quiz.question: A trade feels bad to you. What can you do?
choices: Say no and walk away
Trade anyway even though it feels bad
quiz.explanation: It is okay to say no to a trade that does not feel fair.

slides.title: What is negotiation?
slides.text: Negotiation means talking things out so you both end up happy with the plan. If you want a movie and your sibling wants a game, try movie first, game second.

slides.title: Listen before you ask
slides.text: Listening to what someone wants, and why, helps you find an idea they'll like. If your sibling wants the game because a friend is joining then, watch your movie at that same time.

slides.title: Making a fair trade
slides.text: A fair trade means both people feel like they gained something, not lost it. Doing your sibling's dishes tonight in exchange for picking the movie feels fair to both of you.

slides.title: Splitting the difference
slides.text: When you want thirty extra minutes and your guardian offers ten, you can meet in the middle. Agreeing on twenty minutes is called splitting the difference, and it often feels fair to both sides.

slides.title: Win-win vs. win-lose
slides.text: A win-win means both sides end up happy with the outcome. A win-lose means one side gets everything, and win-lose deals often cause hurt feelings later.

slides.title: Brainstorming options
slides.text: Thinking of two or three ideas, instead of just one, gives you better odds of success. You could suggest watching half the movie now or joining the game after it ends.

slides.title: Staying calm when you disagree
slides.text: Getting upset makes it harder to think clearly and solve the problem. If a talk about TV time gets heated, take a breath and say, "Let's figure this out calmly."

slides.title: Walking away nicely
slides.text: If you truly cannot agree, it is okay to stop and try again later. You could say, "Let's each do something else tonight and talk about it tomorrow."

slides.title: Know what you want first
slides.text: Before you ask for something, figure out what you actually want and why. If you want a later bedtime because of a weekend movie night, say that reason out loud.

slides.title: Negotiating over screen time
slides.text: Screen time is something families often negotiate about, especially between siblings. Agreeing on a schedule, like thirty minutes each, can stop arguments before they start.

slides.title: Splitting chores fairly
slides.text: When two people share a job, splitting it fairly keeps things friendly. One person could vacuum while the other empties the trash, then switch next week.

slides.title: Handling a "no" calmly
slides.text: Sometimes your idea gets turned down, and that is okay. Staying calm and asking a follow-up question works better than arguing.

slides.title: Walking away from a bad trade
slides.text: If a trade does not feel fair to you, you can say no. Walking away from a bad deal is better than agreeing to something you will regret.

quiz.question: You want a movie, your sibling wants a game. What is negotiation?
choices: Talking to find an answer that works for both people
Insisting on getting your own way
quiz.explanation: Negotiation is about finding a solution that works for both sides.

quiz.question: You learn your sibling wants the game because a friend is joining online at a specific time. Why is that helpful to know?
choices: It helps you understand what they want and why
It wastes time
quiz.explanation: Understanding their wants and reasons makes it easier to find an idea they'll accept.

quiz.question: You ask for 30 extra minutes, your guardian offers 10, and you agree on 20. What does "splitting the difference" mean?
choices: Meeting in the middle between two offers
One side getting everything
quiz.explanation: Splitting the difference means landing between the two starting offers.

quiz.question: What is a "win-win" outcome?
choices: Both sides end up happy
One side gets everything and the other gets nothing
quiz.explanation: Win-win means both sides come away satisfied.

quiz.question: Instead of only suggesting one idea for tonight's TV time, you also suggest two backups. Why brainstorm more than one option?
choices: It's more likely you'll find one that works for everyone
One idea is always enough
quiz.explanation: More options make it more likely you'll land on something that works for both sides.

quiz.question: A negotiation over TV time starts to get heated. What helps most?
choices: Staying calm and taking a breath
Getting upset right away
quiz.explanation: Staying calm helps you think more clearly and find a solution.

quiz.question: Before asking for something, what should you figure out first?
choices: What you actually want and why
Nothing, just ask right away
quiz.explanation: Knowing your reason makes your request clearer and stronger.

quiz.question: Two people share a big chore. What helps keep it fair?
choices: Splitting the job and switching tasks later
Only one person doing all of it
quiz.explanation: Splitting the job and taking turns keeps things fair over time.

quiz.question: A trade does not feel fair to you. What can you do?
choices: Say no and walk away
Agree anyway so you do not seem rude
quiz.explanation: It is okay to walk away from a deal that does not feel fair.

slides.title: Interests vs. positions
slides.text: A "position" is what someone says they want ("I want the whole weekend free"). An "interest" is why they want it ("I want time to relax"). Knowing the why opens up more solutions. For example, if a friend's position is "I want to pick the movie every time," but their real interest is "I never get a say in group decisions," understanding that interest could lead to a totally different, better solution — like rotating who picks other group activities too.

slides.title: Preparing before you ask
slides.text: Thinking through what you want, why you want it, and what the other person might say before a conversation makes you far more persuasive. For example, before asking a guardian for a later curfew, thinking through your reason (a friend's event runs late), anticipating their concern (safety getting home), and having an answer ready (a ride arranged) makes your case far stronger than just asking on the spot.

slides.title: Active listening
slides.text: Repeating back what you heard ("so you're saying...") shows the other person you understand them, and often reveals what they actually care about. For example, saying "so you're saying you're worried about how I'll get home safely, not really about the time itself" shows you understood, and might reveal that arranging a safe ride solves their actual concern.

slides.title: Generating multiple options
slides.text: Before agreeing to anything, list a few different possible solutions — the first idea on the table is rarely the best one available. For example, if you're negotiating chore responsibilities with a sibling, rather than accepting the first split suggested, considering two or three different ways to divide the chores often reveals a fairer arrangement than the very first one mentioned.

slides.title: Fair trade-offs
slides.text: If you're asking for something big, offering something in return — like more responsibility for more freedom — makes a deal feel balanced to both sides. For example, asking for a later curfew while also offering to text a check-in halfway through the night makes the request feel like a fair trade instead of a one-sided ask.

slides.title: Managing your emotions
slides.text: Frustration or excitement can push you to agree to a bad deal, or reject a good one. Noticing your own emotions helps you negotiate more clearly. For example, if you're so excited about a trade that you'd agree to almost anything, noticing that excitement and slowing down before agreeing helps you avoid a deal you might regret later.

slides.title: Knowing your walk-away point
slides.text: Deciding in advance what you won't accept helps you avoid agreeing to something you'll regret, even under pressure. For example, deciding beforehand "I won't agree to less than a 10-minute later curfew" helps you stay firm and clear-headed if the conversation gets pushed toward accepting far less.

slides.title: Compromising without losing
slides.text: Compromise isn't losing — it's trading a little of what you want for something that keeps the relationship working well. For example, if you and a friend can't agree on which game to play, agreeing to split the time evenly means neither of you gets everything, but neither of you walks away feeling ignored either.

slides.title: Knowing what you actually want
slides.text: Before you negotiate, get clear on what you really want, separate from what you think you should ask for. For example, if you're negotiating a later curfew, you might realize what you actually want is just one specific late night for a concert, not a permanent change — which makes the ask much easier to agree to.

slides.title: Staying calm when the answer is no
slides.text: Hearing "no" can feel like the conversation is over, but it's often just the start of a longer negotiation. For example, if a guardian says no to a bigger allowance, asking calmly what would need to change for the answer to be yes later keeps the door open instead of shutting it.

slides.title: Negotiating with siblings and friends
slides.text: Negotiating with people you see every day works differently than negotiating with a stranger, because the relationship matters as much as the outcome. For example, winning an argument with a sibling by being harsh might get you the TV tonight, but it can cost you goodwill you'll want the next time you need something from them.

quiz.question: A friend's position is "I want to pick the movie every time," but their interest is "I never get a say." What does this reveal?
choices: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why
They mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Positions are the stated ask; interests are the underlying reason.

quiz.question: Before asking for a later curfew, why think through your reason and anticipate concerns first?
choices: It makes you more persuasive and ready for pushback
Preparing wastes time
quiz.explanation: Thinking it through beforehand makes your case stronger.

quiz.question: You say "so you're saying you're worried about how I'll get home." What does repeating back what you heard show?
choices: That you understand the other person
That you agree with everything they said
quiz.explanation: Active listening shows understanding, not automatic agreement.

quiz.question: Why generate multiple ways to split chores instead of accepting the first suggestion?
choices: The first idea is rarely the best one available
One option is always enough
quiz.explanation: More options increase the odds of finding a genuinely good solution.

quiz.question: Asking for a later curfew while offering to text a check-in halfway through — what does this make the deal feel like?
choices: A fair trade-off, not just a one-sided ask
Getting everything you asked for
quiz.explanation: Offering something in return makes a deal feel fair.

quiz.question: Why decide "I won't accept less than 10 extra minutes" before the conversation even starts?
choices: It helps you avoid agreeing to something you'll regret under pressure
It's not useful to think about
quiz.explanation: Knowing your limit beforehand protects you from a bad deal made in the moment.

quiz.question: When you compromise with a friend over which game to play, what actually happens?
choices: You trade a little of what you want to keep things working well
One person always gets everything they want
quiz.explanation: Compromise means giving up a little, not giving up entirely.

quiz.question: A guardian says no to a bigger allowance. What is a good next step?
choices: Calmly ask what would need to change for a yes later
Give up on the topic completely
quiz.explanation: A "no" is often the start of a longer conversation, not the end.

quiz.question: A trade a friend offers is clearly unfair to you. What is a reasonable response?
choices: Say you'd rather keep what you have
Accept it so you don't seem difficult
quiz.explanation: Walking away from an unfair deal is a reasonable, healthy choice.

slides.title: Positions vs. interests
slides.text: A position is what someone says they want. An interest is the deeper reason behind it. Two people can hold different positions but share the same interest, and that's where good deals get found. For example, in a group project, one partner's position might be "I'll write it myself," while another's is "I want more input" — yet both share the same interest: wanting the project to succeed.

slides.title: Your BATNA
slides.text: Your BATNA is simply your backup plan — what you'll do if this deal falls through. A strong backup plan gives you real power, because you never have to accept a bad deal out of desperation. For example, having another job offer lined up gives you the confidence to walk away from a lowball wage.

slides.title: Anchoring
slides.text: Anchoring means the first number mentioned in a negotiation shapes everything that follows, often without anyone noticing it. That's why it usually pays to make a well-researched first offer instead of waiting to react to someone else's. For example, opening an allowance talk with "fifteen dollars a week feels fair, based on my chores" sets the anchor for the whole conversation.

slides.title: Principled negotiation
slides.text: Principled negotiation means separating the person from the problem. You stay warm and respectful toward someone while still being firm about the actual issue you disagree on. For example, telling a partner "I really value working with you, and I also think we need firmer deadlines" does both at once.

slides.title: Distributive negotiation
slides.text: In a distributive negotiation, there's a fixed amount to split, so one side's gain is the other side's loss. For example, splitting a single $100 prize between two people is distributive — every extra dollar you get is a dollar your friend doesn't.

slides.title: Expanding the pie
slides.text: Some negotiations aren't fixed at all — there's room to expand the pie so both sides end up better off. For example, a job offer with salary, remote days, and vacation time lets you trade across categories instead of fighting over just one number.

slides.title: Reading emotional signals
slides.text: Reading emotional signals means noticing hesitation, discomfort, or excitement in the other person, not just their words. For example, if someone tenses up the moment a certain topic comes up, that reaction itself is telling you something their words aren't.

slides.title: Negotiating ethically
slides.text: Being honest, and not taking advantage of someone's inexperience or urgency, isn't just the kind thing to do. It's also what makes people willing to negotiate with you again in the future. For example, telling a buyer honestly that an item is worth less than they're offering builds trust that pays off later.

slides.title: Where this shows up in real life
slides.text: Negotiation isn't just for salaries — it shows up when splitting rent, dividing a group project's workload, or pricing something you're selling. For example, deciding who takes the smaller bedroom for lower rent with a future roommate uses the same interests-and-trade-offs thinking as negotiating a job offer.

slides.title: Knowing what you actually want
slides.text: Before you negotiate anything, get honest with yourself about what you actually want, separate from what you assume you should ask for. For example, you might ask for a later curfew when what you really want is just one late night for a specific event.

slides.title: Handling "no" without giving up
slides.text: A "no" usually isn't the end of a negotiation — it's just information about where the other person stands right now. For example, asking calmly "what would need to change for this to become a yes" keeps the conversation open instead of shutting it down.

slides.title: Negotiating with people you're close to
slides.text: Negotiating with a sibling or close friend works differently than negotiating with a stranger, because the relationship itself is worth protecting. For example, winning an argument by being harsh might get you what you want tonight, but it can cost you trust you'll need later.

slides.title: The walk-away point
slides.text: Deciding in advance what you absolutely won't accept — your walk-away point — protects you from agreeing to something you'll regret under pressure. For example, deciding beforehand "I won't work for less than $12 an hour" keeps you firm if an employer tries to push you lower.

slides.title: Compromise isn't the same as losing
slides.text: A real compromise means both sides give up something small to gain something bigger — it isn't the same as losing. For example, agreeing to split a shared expense evenly, even if you originally wanted the other person to cover more, can still leave both sides satisfied.

quiz.question: Two group project partners want different things but share the interest of wanting a great final product. Why focus on interests?
choices: Different positions can share the same underlying interest, opening up solutions
Positions and interests are always identical
quiz.explanation: Focusing on the underlying interest reveals options a stated position hides.

quiz.question: You have a backup job offer while negotiating pay for another job. What is that backup called?
choices: Your BATNA — best alternative if the deal falls through
The first offer made in a negotiation
quiz.explanation: BATNA stands for Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement.

quiz.question: Opening an allowance negotiation with a well-researched "$15 a week" tends to shape the rest of the talk. What is this called?
choices: Anchoring — the first offer shapes the rest of the conversation
It has no effect on what follows
quiz.explanation: Anchoring means the first number shapes expectations for the rest of the talk.

quiz.question: Telling a partner "I value working with you, and I also think we need firmer deadlines." What does this show?
choices: Principled negotiation — separating the people from the problem
Being aggressive toward the other person
quiz.explanation: It means staying warm to the person while being firm about the issue.

quiz.question: Splitting a fixed $100 prize between two people, where one's gain is the other's loss, is what kind of negotiation?
choices: A distributive negotiation
One where both sides can always expand the pie
quiz.explanation: A distributive negotiation splits a fixed amount, unlike one where the pie can grow.

quiz.question: Someone hesitates specifically when a certain topic comes up in a negotiation. What can that reveal?
choices: What they actually value most
Nothing useful
quiz.explanation: Emotional signals often reveal priorities that words alone don't.

quiz.question: You point out honestly that a buyer doesn't realize an item's real value, instead of exploiting that. Why negotiate this way?
choices: It's what makes people willing to negotiate with you again
Ethics don't matter once a deal is signed
quiz.explanation: Fair dealing builds the trust needed for future negotiations.

quiz.question: Your guardian says no to a request. What's a better response than giving up?
choices: Calmly ask what would need to change for a future yes
Immediately stop asking about anything related to it forever
quiz.explanation: A "no" often signals where things stand now, not that the door is closed forever.

quiz.question: Deciding beforehand "I won't accept less than $12 an hour" before a job negotiation. What is this called?
choices: Your walk-away point, decided before the negotiation starts
Something you only figure out after the negotiation ends
quiz.explanation: A walk-away point is a limit you set for yourself in advance, before pressure sets in.

quiz.question: Two people split a shared expense evenly, even though one originally wanted the other to pay more. What does this show?
choices: A real compromise — both sides give up something small to gain something bigger
One side completely losing the negotiation
quiz.explanation: Compromise means both sides give a little, which isn't the same as losing.
